Early Curiosity and the Seeds of a Lifelong Obsession.
Have you ever felt that restless spark as a kid—that itch to figure out how things really work? For one boy growing up in the American heartland, that curiosity wasn’t just a passing phase. In his family, numbers and stories mixed right in with the mashed potatoes at dinner. His dad, who ran a local business and later served in Congress, would come home with lively stories about markets and politics. Meanwhile, his mom’s quick wit and high expectations set the tone for everything.
This boy wasn’t loud or showy. Instead, he watched. He listened. And he got hooked on the logic tucked inside numbers—the idea that, if you looked closely enough, you could find order in all the chaos around you. He’d spend hours with books, not just memorizing baseball stats or horse racing odds, but searching for patterns—tiny clues that hinted at something bigger. He realized early on: the world rewards people who notice what everyone else overlooks.
His first ventures were simple, but they lit a fire. Picture a kid just tall enough to peek over the counter, buying packs of gum and bottles of soda, then walking door-to-door to sell them around the neighborhood. Sure, watching his pile of coins grow felt great. But even more satisfying was the challenge—figuring out what neighbors wanted, what they’d pay, and how to make each sale a little better than the last. Those small wins taught him early lessons: patience, persistence, and the magic of watching tiny gains add up over time.
School was a different story. The classroom routines sometimes felt stifling, but the library? Now that was a haven. There, curiosity could run wild. He devoured stories about famous investors and self-made millionaires, learning how fortunes were built—and lost. These weren’t just fun tales. They were blueprints, maps to a world he desperately wanted to join.
Back at home, the family’s ups and downs mirrored the wild swings of the Great Depression. Money was never just a given. He watched his dad handle setbacks with quiet grit, never bending his principles. Integrity, he realized, wasn’t just about being good—it was smart business. People remembered how you treated them, and once you lost their trust, it was almost impossible to win it back.
As he got older, his interests sharpened. He started tracking stock prices, filling notebooks with careful notes. Using money he’d saved from odd jobs, he made his first investments—sticking with companies he understood, ones that made things he could see and touch. The thrill of seeing his money grow? That was incredible. But what really hooked him was the process—the research, the waiting, the discipline it took to get things right.
Most folks, he noticed, wanted everything fast—quick results, easy wins. But he saw that true success was a long game. It was like rolling a snowball down a hill: it starts slow, but give it time and those gains start to build up, faster and faster.
That’s how the seeds of a lifelong obsession were planted. He wasn’t just learning about money—he was discovering what really mattered to him. Curiosity, patience, and integrity—these were the qualities that would shape the rest of his life.
